<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def.PCG}
A \emph{pairwise compatibility graph} (PCG) is a graph $G$ for which there exist a weighted tree $T$, whose edges have positive real weights, and an interval $I$ of nonnegative real numbers, such that
$V(G)=L(T)$ and, for every two distinct leaves $u,v\in L(T)$,
$uv\in E(G)$  if and only if $d_T(u,v)\in I$ (where $d_T(u,v)$ denotes the weighted distance between $u$ and $v$ in $T$).
In this case, $T$ is called a witness tree of $G$ and we denote $G=PCG(T,I).$
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:cat_PCGs}
For non-negative integers $0\leq a\leq b$, we denote by $\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}$ the class of graphs $G$ for which $G=\mathrm{PCG}(T,[a,b])$ for some unweighted caterpillar $T$.
We define
\[
\mathrm{Cat\mbox{-}PCG}
   =\bigcup_{0\leq a\leq b}\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}.
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:ab-labelling}
Let $a, b$ be two non-negative integers with $ 0\leq a\leq b $. An \emph{$ [a,b] $-difference labelling} of $ G $ is a function $ p\colon V(G)\to \mathbb{N} $ such that $ uv\in E(G) $ if and only if $ |p(u)-p(v)|\in [a,b] $.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:char}
Let $G$ be a graph and let $a,b$ be two non-negative integers with $0\leq a\leq b$. Then $G\in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a+2,b+2)}$  if and only if $G$ admits an $[a,b]$-difference labelling.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Suppose first $G=PCG(T,[a+2,b+2])$ then for any two distinct vertices $u,v$ we have that $uv\in E(G)$ if and only if $|\pi_T(u)-\pi_T(v)|\in [a,b]$ which means that $\pi_T$ is an $[a,b]$-difference labelling. 

Conversely, given an $[a,b]$-difference labelling $p$, let $c=\min_{v\in V(G)} p(v)$ and define for every $v$, $q(v)=p(v)-c+1$. This is just a shifting of the labels so they start from $1$. Notice that $q$ is again an $[a,b]$-labelling as $|q(v)-q(u)|=|p(v)- p(u)|$.  Now, let $r=\max_{v\in V(G)} q(v)$,and take a path$ s_1,\dots,s_r$, and attach each vertex $v\in V(G)$ as a leaf to $s_{q(v)}$. The resulting tree is a caterpillar and satisfies $d_T(u,v)=|p(u)-p(v)|+2$ for all distinct $u,v$. Hence it is a witness for $G$ with interval $[a+2,b+2]$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- observation-1: body_md -->
\label{obs:same_label_twins}
Let \(G\) have an \([a,b]\)-difference labelling \(p\). If \(p(u)=p(v)\) for two distinct vertices \(u,v\), then \(u\) and \(v\) are twins. More precisely, they are false twins if \(a>0\), and true twins if \(a=0\).  In particular, if $G$ is twin-free then $p$ is injective.
<!-- end observation-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:close}
Let \(0\leq a\leq b\). The class of graphs admitting an
\([a,b]\)-difference labelling is closed under:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item taking induced subgraphs;
    \item taking disjoint unions;
    \item adding false twins, when \(a>0\);
    \item adding true twins, when \(a=0\).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
An induced subgraph inherits the restriction of the original
labelling. For the disjoint union of two graphs, translate all labels of one component sufficiently far to the right so that every
difference between vertices of distinct components is larger than
\(b\). Finally, a twin of a vertex \(u\) can be assigned the same label as \(u\). The two vertices then have the same neighbours outside the pair. Their mutual difference is zero, so they are nonadjacent when \(a>0\) and adjacent when \(a=0\).
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:tww_cat}
Every graph in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\) has twin-width at most \(10\).
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let \(G'\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\). By Theorem~\ref{thm:char}, \(G'\) admits an
\([a,b]\)-difference labelling $p$.

If two vertices receive the same label, then they are twins by
Observation~\ref{obs:same_label_twins}. Merging vertices with the same label
does not create any mixed pair, since all vertices in such a class have the same
adjacency to every vertex outside the class. Therefore, it is enough to consider
the case where $p$ is injective.

By shifting all labels if necessary, assume that \(p(v)\geq 1\) for every
\(v\in V(G')\). Let \(n\) be a power of two such that
\[
n\geq \max\{p(v):v\in V(G')\}.
\]
Let \(G\) be the graph with vertex set \([n]\), where
\[
ij\in E(G)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
|i-j|\in [a,b].
\]
Then \(G'\) is an induced subgraph of \(G\). Since twin-width does not increase
when taking induced subgraphs, it is enough to give a contraction sequence for
\(G\) of width at most \(10\).

We use a contraction sequence that repeatedly merges consecutive pairs of
intervals. At every step, the current parts are intervals of \([n]\). Initially,
\[
\mathcal I=([1],[2],\ldots,[n]).
\]
In the first round, we merge consecutive pairs \([1]\) with \([2]\), \([3]\)
with \([4]\), and so on. In the next round, we merge consecutive pairs of the
new intervals, and we continue in this way until only one interval remains.

Thus, at the beginning of round \(t\), every interval has size \(2^{t-1}\).
During round \(t\), we process the intervals from left to right. Hence, at any
intermediate step of the round, the current interval partition consists of
intervals of size \(2^t\) in the processed prefix and intervals of size
\(2^{t-1}\) in the unprocessed suffix.

We show that every current interval has mixed degree at most \(10\). Consider
an intermediate partition
\[
\mathcal I^*=(I_1,\ldots,I_\ell),
\]
and fix an interval
\[
I_c=[q,r].
\]
Let \(\delta=r-q\). Hence
\[
|I_c|=\delta+1\in\{2^{t-1},2^t\}.
\]

First consider intervals to the right of \(I_c\). Let \(I_d\) be such an
interval. If all distances between vertices of \(I_c\) and vertices of \(I_d\)
are smaller than \(a\), then there is no edge between \(I_c\) and \(I_d\). If
all such distances lie in \([a,b]\), then all possible edges between \(I_c\) and
\(I_d\) are present. If all such distances are larger than \(b\), then again
there is no edge between \(I_c\) and \(I_d\).

Therefore \(I_c\) and \(I_d\) can be mixed only when \(I_d\) intersects one of
the two boundary zones
\[
[q+a,r+a]
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
[q+b,r+b].
\]
Each of these zones has size \(|I_c|\leq 2^t\), while every current interval has
size at least \(2^{t-1}\). Hence each boundary zone intersects at most three
intervals of \(\mathcal I^*\). Thus \(I_c\) has at most \(6\) mixed neighbours
to its right.

Now consider intervals to the left of \(I_c\). The same argument shows that
mixed neighbours to the left can occur only among intervals intersecting one of
the two boundary zones
\[
[q-a,r-a]
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
[q-b,r-b].
\]
We claim that each of these zones intersects at most two intervals to the left.
If \(|I_c|=2^{t-1}\), then the zone has size \(2^{t-1}\), and every current
interval has size at least \(2^{t-1}\). If \(|I_c|=2^t\), then \(I_c\) lies in
the processed prefix, and all intervals to its left also have size \(2^t\),
because contractions are performed from left to right. Thus, in either case,
each boundary zone contributes at most two intervals. Therefore \(I_c\) has at
most \(4\) mixed neighbours to its left.

Finally, every current interval has mixed degree at most $6+4=10$. Thus this contraction sequence has width at most \(10\). Hence every graph in
\(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\) has twin-width at most \(10\).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\cite{brandsadt2008ptolemaic}\label{theo:unit_inerval}
Every unit interval graph is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
Every caterpillar is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $T$ be a caterpillar.
The cases \(|V(T)|\leq 2\) are immediate, so assume $|V(T)| \geq 3$. Assume also that the
spine of \(T\) is the path $s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_k$ ordered from left to right. For every \(i\in[k]\), let \(L_i\) be the
set of leaves adjacent to \(s_i\). Set $M=2k+1$ and, for every \(i\in[k]\), define $c_i=k-i+1$. Thus, $c_1=k,\quad c_2=k-1,\quad\ldots,\quad c_k=1$. Define
$$
p(v)=
\begin{cases}
1+(i-1)M, \textrm{ if $v=s_i$ where $s_i$ is a spine vertex, }\\
1+iM-c_i, \textrm{ if $v=x$ where  \(x\in L_i\).}
\end{cases}
$$
\noindent
We prove that \(p\) is a \([k+1,M]\)-difference labelling of \(T\). First, consider the edges of \(T\). If \(s_i s_{i+1}\) is a spine
edge, then  $|p(s_{i+1})-p(s_i)|=M \in [k+1,M]$. Next, for any edge $(x, s_i)$, with $x \in L_i$, we have  $|p(x)-p(s_i)|=M-c_i \in [k+1,M]$ as $1 \leq c_i \leq k $. 


We now show that no non-edge has label difference in this interval. If \(s_i\) and \(s_j\) are not consecutive spine vertices, then
$|p(s_i)-p(s_j)|=|i-j|M\geq 2M>M$. If \(x,y\in L_i\), then \(p(x)=p(y)\), and hence $|p(x)-p(y)|=0<k+1$. Next, let \(x\in L_i\), and consider a spine vertex \(s_j\neq s_i\).
If \(j=i+1\), then $|p(s_{i+1})-p(x)|=c_i\leq k$. If \(j\leq i-1\), then  $|p(x)-p(s_j)|=(i-j+1)M-c_i \geq 2M-k>M$. If \(j\geq i+2\), then $|p(s_j)-p(x)|=(j-i-1)M+c_i>M$. Finally, let \(x\in L_i\) and \(y\in L_j\), where \(i<j\). Then $p(y)-p(x)=(j-i)M+c_i-c_j$.
Since $c_i-c_j=j-i$, we obtain $p(y)-p(x)=(j-i)(M+1)>M$.

Thus \(p\) is a \([k+1,2k+1]\)-difference labelling of \(T\).
By Theorem~1, $T\in \mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG}(k+3,2k+3)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{theo:cycles}
For every $n\ge 3$, the cycle $C_n$ is a \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}. More specifically,
$C_3\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(2,2)} $, and for every $ n\ge4$,
 $C_n\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(5,7)}$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The statement for $C_3$ is immediate, since $C_3$ is complete and thus
admits a $[0,0]$-difference labelling.

Let $n\ge4 $. By Theorem~\ref{thm:char}, it suffices to construct a
$[3,5]$-difference labelling of $C_n$.

Assume first that $n=2k$ is even. Let the vertices of $C_n$ be
$(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_{2k-1})$ in cyclic order and define
$$
p(v_i)=
\begin{cases}
1, & i=0,\\
4i, & 1\le i\le k-1,\\
4k+1, & i=k,\\
4(2k-i)+2, & k+1\le i\le 2k-1.
\end{cases}
$$

Thus the labels around the cycle are:
$$
1,4,8,\ldots,4k-4,4k+1,4k-2,4k-6,\ldots,6.
$$

Consecutive vertices on the cycle have label difference $3$, $4$, or $5$,
and hence every edge of $C_n$ corresponds to a difference in $[3,5]$.

To prove the converse, observe that all labels except $1$ and $4k+1$
belong to one of the arithmetic progressions
$$
4,8,\ldots,4k-4,
\qquad
6,10,\ldots,4k-2,
$$
both having common difference $4$.
Therefore, for two distinct labels different from $1$ and $4k+1$, a
difference in $[3,5]$ can only be equal to $4$, which occurs precisely
between consecutive terms of one of the two progressions. By construction,
these pairs are exactly edges of the cycle.

Moreover, the only labels at distance in $[3,5]$ from $1$ are $4$ and
$6$, while the only labels at distance in $[3,5]$ from $4k+1$ are
$4k-4$ and $4k-2$. These are exactly the four neighbours of the
corresponding vertices on the cycle.

Hence
$$
v_iv_j\in E(C_n)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
|p(v_i)-p(v_j)|\in[3,5],
$$
and $p$ is a $[3,5]$-difference labelling of $C_n$.

The odd case $n=2k+1$ is identical. Define
$$
p(v_i)=
\begin{cases}
1, & i=0,\\
4i, & 1\le i\le k,\\
4k+3, & i=k+1,\\
4(2k+1-i)+2, & k+2\le i\le 2k.
\end{cases}
$$

The labels are
$$
1,4,8,\ldots,4k,4k+3,4k-2,4k-6,\ldots,6.
$$

Again, consecutive vertices have differences $3$, $4$, or $5$. As before,
all labels except $1$ and $4k+3$ belong to two arithmetic progressions of
difference $4$, so the only pairs with difference in $[3,5]$ are
consecutive terms of one of these progressions together with the pairs
$$
{1,4},\ {1,6},\ {4k+3,4k},\ {4k+3,4k-2}.
$$
These are precisely the edges of the cycle.

Therefore $p$ is a $[3,5]$-difference labelling of $C_n$, and hence
$C_n\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(5,7)}$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:skewed grid}
For any $n, m\in \mathbb{N}$, the $n \times m$ skewed grid is a \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(n+3,n+4)}.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $G$ be the $n\times m$ skewed grid. For a vertex $(i,j)$, set
$r=j-n+i$. Notice that $r\in[m]$. Define $p(i,j)=(r-1)(n+1)+i.$
Equivalently, $p(i,j)=(j-n+i-1)(n+1)+i$. We claim that $p$ is an $[n+1,n+2]$-difference labelling. Let
$(i,j)$ and $(i',j')$ be two distinct vertices, and set
$r=j-n+i$, $r'=j'-n+i'$.
Assume without loss of generality that $p(i',j')>p(i,j)$. Then
$$
p(i',j')-p(i,j)=(r'-r)(n+1)+(i'-i).
$$
Since $i,i'\in[n]$, we have
$$
-(n-1)\leq i'-i\leq n-1.
$$
\noindent
If $p(i',j')-p(i,j)=n+1$, then necessarily $r'-r=1$ and $i'-i=0$. Hence $i'=i$ and $r'=r+1$, which means $j'=j+1$. Thus the two vertices are adjacent in the same row.

\noindent
Otherwise if $ p(i',j')-p(i,j)=n+2$, then necessarily $r'-r=1$ and $i'-i=1$. Hence $i'=i+1$, and since
$j'=n-i'+r'=n-(i+1)+(r+1)=n-i+r=j$,
the two vertices are adjacent in the same column.

Conversely, if two vertices are adjacent in the same row, say $(i,j)$ and $(i,j+1)$, then their labels differ by $n+1$. If two vertices are adjacent in the same column, say $(i,j)$ and $(i+1,j)$, then their labels differ by $n+2$.

Therefore two vertices are adjacent exactly when their label difference belongs to
$[n+1,n+2]$. Hence $p$ is an $[n+1,n+2]$-difference labelling of $G$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
For every $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, the $n \times m$ grid is a \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(n+3,n+4)}.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:add_small_components}
Let $0\leq a\leq b$ with $b\geq 2$, and let
$G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}$. Then
$G\dot\cup K_1$, $G\dot\cup K_2$ and $G\dot\cup \overline{K_2}$
also belong to $\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Since the distance between any two distinct leaves of an unweighted tree is at least $2$, if $a<2$ then
$\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(2,b)}$. Thus, assume $a\geq 2$ and set $A=a-2$ and $B=b-2$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:char}, $G$ admits an $[A,B]$-difference labelling. Clearly $K_1$ admits an $[A,B]$-difference labelling. If $A>0$, label the vertices of $K_2$ by $1,1+A$ and those of $\overline{K_2}$ by $1,1$. If $A=0$, use respectively the labels $1,1$ and $1,B+2$.

Thus $K_1$, $K_2$, and $\overline{K_2}$ admit an $[A,B]$-difference labelling. The claim follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:close} and Theorem~\ref{thm:char}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{theo:five_vertices}
Every graph on at most five vertices is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The connected graphs on at most five vertices are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:connected_graphs_at_most_five},
together with explicit difference labellings. Let $G$ be disconnected. If $G$ has a connected component $H$ with at least three vertices, then $G-H$ has at most two vertices. Hence $G$ is obtained from $H$ by adding $K_1$, $K_2$, or
$\overline{K_2}$, and the result follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:add_small_components}. Otherwise, every component of $G$ is either $K_1$ or $K_2$. Since both admit a $[1,1]$-difference labelling, repeated application of Proposition~\ref{prop:close} shows that $G$ also admits a $[1,1]$-difference labelling. Hence $G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:char}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:betweenness_obstruction}
Let $G$ have an $[a,b]$-difference labelling $p$, and let
$x,u,v,w\in V(G)$ be distinct vertices such that $xu,xw\in E(G)$. If either
\[
p(x)\leq p(u)<p(v)<p(w),
\]
or
\[
p(u)<p(v)<p(w)\leq p(x),
\]
then \(xv\in E(G)\).
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We prove the first case; the second follows by reversing the order of the line. Since \(xu,xw\in E(G)\), we have
$a\leq p(u)-p(x)$  and $p(w)-p(x)\leq b.$
Moreover, $p(u)-p(x)\leq p(v)-p(x)\leq p(w)-p(x).$
Thus
$a\leq p(v)-p(x)\leq b,$ and hence \(xv\in E(G)\).
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:corollary_betweeness}
Let \(p(u)<p(v)<p(w)\). If a vertex \(x\) is adjacent to \(u\)
and \(w\), but not to \(v\), then
\[
p(u)<p(x)<p(w).
\]
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:inclusion_neigborhood}
Let $G=(V,E)$ have an $ [a,b] $-difference labelling $p$. Let $u_1,u_2,u_3\in V$ be distinct vertices such that $p(u_1)\le p(u_2)\le p(u_3)$ and  $p(u_3)-p(u_1)\le b-a$.  Then $N(u_2)\subseteq N(u_1)\cup N(u_3).$
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
For simplicity we first set:
\[
\alpha=p(u_2)-p(u_1),\qquad \beta=p(u_3)-p(u_2).
\]
Then $\alpha,\beta\ge 0$, and by assumption $\alpha+\beta=p(u_3)-p(u_1)\le b-a.$

Now, let $x\in N(u_2)$. Then $a\le |p(x)-p(u_2)|\le b.$ We need to consider the following cases:

\paragraph{Case I: $p(x)\ge p(u_2)$.}  Then  let $d=p(x)-p(u_2)$ and clearly  $a\le d \le b$. Now 

\begin{itemize}
    \item Suppose $d\ge a+\beta$. Then $a\le d-\beta \leq d$  but as 
$d-\beta=p(x)-p(u_2)+p(u_2)-p(u_3)=p(x)-p(u_3)$, we have that $p(x)-p(u_3) \in [a,b]$ thus, $x\in N(u_3)$.
    \item Suppose $d<a+\beta$.  Then $a \le d+\alpha < a+\alpha+\beta\le a+(b-a)=b$ but $d+\alpha= p(x)-p(u_2)+p(u_2)-p(u_1)=p(x)-p(u_1)$. Thus, we have that $p(x)-p(u_1) \in [a,b]$ thus, $x\in N(u_1)$.
\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Case II: $p(x) < p(u_2)$.}  Then  let $d=p(u_2)-p(x)$ and again we have  $a\le d \le b$. Now,

\begin{itemize}
    \item Suppose $d\ge a+\alpha$. Then $a\le d-\alpha\le b$ but as $d-\alpha= p(u_2)-p(x)+p(u_1)-p(u_2)=p(u_1)-p(x)$ we have $p(u_1)-p(x) \in [a,b]$ thus, $x\in N(u_1)$.
    \item Suppose $d<a+\alpha$.  Then $a\le d+\beta<a+\alpha+\beta\le a+(b-a)\le b$ but as $d+\beta=p(u_2)-p(x) + p(u_3)-p(u_2)= p(u_3)-p(x)$. Thus, we have that $p(u_3) -p(x) \in [a,b]$ thus, $x\in N(u_3)$.
\end{itemize}


Therefore every neighbor $x$ of $u_2$ belongs to
$N(u_1)\cup N(u_3)$. Hence $N(u_2)\subseteq N(u_1)\cup N(u_3).$
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{theo:tree_cat_pcgs}
The subdivided star $S_{2,2,2,2,2}$, depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:graphs-section4}(a), is not a Cat-PCG.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Suppose, to the contrary, that $S_{2,2,2,2,2}$ admits an $[a,b]$-difference labelling $p$. Consider the center $r$, whose neighbors are $u_1,\dots,u_5$. At least three of these neighbors lie on the same side of $p(r)$. Assume
$ p(r)\leq p(u_1)\leq p(u_2)\leq p(u_3)$ (the other case  $p(u_1)\leq p(u_2)\leq p(u_3) \leq p(r)$ is symmetric).  Since $r$ is adjacent to $u_1,u_2,u_3$, we have $a\leq p(u_i)-p(r)\leq b$ for all $i=1,2,3$.  In particular, $p(u_3) - p(r) \leq b$ and $p(u_1) - p(r) \geq a$. Hence $p(u_3)-p(u_1)\leq b-a$. Thus, the vertices $u_1,u_2$ and $u_3$ satisfy the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem:inclusion_neigborhood} and thus it must hold that $N(u_2)\subseteq N(u_1)\cup N(u_3).$
But $u_2$ has a private leaf $\ell_2$, adjacent to $u_2$ and to neither $u_1$ nor $u_3$ reaching a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:trees}
Not every tree is a Cat-PCG.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:cube_not_cat}
The cube graph \(Q_3\) depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:graphs-section4}(b) is not in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\).
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Suppose, on the contrary that \(Q_3\) admits an \([a,b]\)-difference labelling \(p\). 
Since \(Q_3\) is twin-free, Observation~\ref{obs:same_label_twins} implies that \(p\) is injective. Let \(u\) be the vertex with minimum label. Let
$N(u)=\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$, where $p(v_1)<p(v_2)<p(v_3).$

We first claim that no vertex different from \(v_2\) can have a label strictly between \(p(v_1)\) and \(p(v_3)\). Indeed, suppose that there exists a vertex \(y\neq v_2\) such that
$p(v_1)<p(y)<p(v_3).$ Because the inequalities are strict and $y \neq v_1, v_3$ and by assumption $y\neq v_2$ we have \(y\notin \{v_1,v_2,v_3\}=N(u)\). Since $u$ has the minimum label then $p(u)< p(v_1) < p(y) < p(v_3)$ and $u$ is adjacent to $v_1$ and $v_3$. Thus, we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:betweenness_obstruction} with \(u\)
as the distinguished vertex and \(v_1,y,v_3\) as the ordered
triple and we obtain $uy \in E(Q_3)$ which contradicts $y \notin N(u)$.


We now use the structure of the cube. Represent the vertices of
\(Q_3\) by binary strings of length three, with two vertices adjacent if and only if they differ in exactly one coordinate. We may assume that $u=000$. Therefore, $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}=\{100,010,001\}$, where the indices \(1,2,3\) are determined by the ordering $p(v_1)<p(v_2)<p(v_3)$. Let \(x\) be the vertex obtained by taking the bitwise OR of the binary strings corresponding to \(v_1\) and \(v_3\). Then \(x\) is adjacent to both \(v_1\) and \(v_3\), but not to \(v_2\). Since $p(v_1)<p(v_2)<p(v_3)$, Corollary~\ref{cor:corollary_betweeness} implies that
$p(v_1)<p(x)<p(v_3)$. Moreover, \(x\neq v_2\), contradicting the claim above.

Therefore, $Q_3\notin\mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG}$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:high_dimensional_grids}
Let \(G\) be a \(d\)-dimensional grid. If at least three side lengths of \(G\) are greater than \(1\), then \(G\notin\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\).
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{theo:w6}
The wheel graph \(W_6\) depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:graphs-section4}(c) is not in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\).
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let \(u\) be the center of \(W_6\), and let the other five vertices induce a
cycle \(C_5\). Suppose, on the contrary that \(W_6\) admits an
\([a,b]\)-difference labelling \(p\). Since \(W_6\) is twin-free, from 
Observation~\ref{obs:same_label_twins} we have that \(p\) is injective.

Since \(u\) is adjacent to the five vertices of the cycle, at least three of
them lie on the same side of \(p(u)\). Wlog let
\(v_1,v_2,v_3\) be the first three cycle vertices to the right of \(u\) (the case when they are on the left is symmetric), so that
$$
p(u)<p(v_1)<p(v_2)<p(v_3).
$$
Let \(r,s\) be the two remaining cycle vertices. By the choice of
\(v_1,v_2,v_3\), neither \(r\) nor \(s\) lies in the interval
\((p(u),p(v_3))\).

Notice that subgraph induced by \(\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}\) in the cycle \(C_5\) has either one edge or two edges.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 1.} Suppose \(C_5[\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}]\) has exactly one edge.
Then one among \(v_1,v_2,v_3\) is isolated in this induced subgraph. In a \(5\)-cycle, each of the two remaining vertices \(r,s\) is adjacent to this isolated vertex and to exactly one endpoint of the unique edge. Hence there exist
\(x\in\{r,s\}\) and indices \(i<j\) such that
$$
xv_i\notin E(W_6)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
xv_j\in E(W_6).
$$
Clearly,  \(x\) is also adjacent to \(u\). Applying
Corollary~\ref{cor:corollary_betweeness} to the triple
\((u,v_i,v_j)\) and the vertex \(x\), we obtain
$$
p(u)<p(x)<p(v_j)\leq p(v_3),
$$
contradicting the  fact that neither \(r\) nor \(s\) lies in the interval
\((p(u),p(v_3))\).

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Case 2.} Suppose \(C_5[\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}]\) has exactly two edges.
This means that these three vertices induce a path. In a \(5\)-cycle, each of the two remaining vertices \(r,s\) is adjacent to exactly one endpoint of this path and to neither its middle vertex. Hence again there exist \(x\in\{r,s\}\) and
indices \(i<j\) such that
$$
xv_i\notin E(W_6)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
xv_j\in E(W_6).
$$
As before, \(xu\in E(W_6)\). Applying
Corollary~\ref{cor:corollary_betweeness} to \((u,v_i,v_j)\) and \(x\), we get
$$
p(u)<p(x)<p(v_j)\leq p(v_3),
$$
again contradicting the  fact that neither \(r\) nor \(s\) lies in the interval
\((p(u),p(v_3))\).

In both cases we obtain a contradiction. Therefore \(W_6\notin\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\).
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:co_sunlet3_not_cat}
The graph \( \overline{\emph{sunlet}_3} \) depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:graphs-section4}(d) is not in \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\).
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let \(G=\overline{\emph{sunlet}_3}\). We denote its vertices by
$\{v_1,v_2,v_3,w_1,w_2,w_3\}$, where \(v_1,v_2,v_3\) induce a clique, \(w_1,w_2,w_3\) induce an independent set, and $v_iw_j\in E(G)$ if and only if  $i\neq j.$ Thus \(v_iw_i\notin E(G)\) for each \(i\).

Suppose, on the contrary that \(G\) admits an \([a,b]\)-difference labelling \(p\). Since \(G\) is twin-free, Observation~\ref{obs:same_label_twins} implies that \(p\) is injective. Relabelling if necessary, assume
$$
p(v_1)<p(v_2)<p(v_3).
$$

Now \(w_2\) is adjacent to \(v_1\) and \(v_3\), but not to \(v_2\). By Corollary~\ref{cor:corollary_betweeness}, we get $p(v_1)<p(w_2)<p(v_3).$
Hence either \(p(w_2)<p(v_2)\) or \(p(v_2)<p(w_2)\).

Suppose first that $p(v_1)<p(w_2)<p(v_2).$ The vertex \(w_3\) is adjacent to \(v_1\) and \(v_2\), but not to \(w_2\). Applying Corollary~\ref{cor:corollary_betweeness} to the triple \((v_1,w_2,v_2)\) and the vertex \(w_3\), we obtain $p(v_1)<p(w_3)<p(v_2).$ But \(v_3\) is adjacent to \(v_1\) and \(v_2\), and not adjacent to \(w_3\). Applying the same lemma again to \((v_1,w_3,v_2)\) and \(v_3\), we get $p(v_1)<p(v_3)<p(v_2),$ contradicting $p(v_2)<p(v_3)$.

The case $p(v_2)<p(w_2)<p(v_3)$  is symmetric. Indeed, using \(w_1\) in place of \(w_3\), the lemma first gives $p(v_2)<p(w_1)<p(v_3)$, and then, using \(v_1\), gives $p(v_2)<p(v_1)<p(v_3)$,
contradicting \(p(v_1)<p(v_2)\).

Therefore no such difference labelling exists, and hence \(G\notin\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}\).
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:centipede_characterization}
Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices. Then $G$ has a centipede witness with interval
$[a,b]$ if and only if $G$ is isomorphic to $P_n^{\,b-2}-P_n^{\,a-3}$.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Suppose first that \(G\) has a centipede witness \(T\) with interval \([a,b]\). Let
\(s_1,\dots,s_n\) be the spine vertices in order, and let \(v_i\) be the unique leaf adjacent to
\(s_i\). Then, for \(i<j\), $d_T(v_i,v_j)=j-i+2$. Therefore $v_iv_j\in E(G)$
if and only if $j-i+2\in [a,b]$ or equivalently  $j-i\in [a-2,b-2]$.
Thus $G$ is isomorphic to $P_n^{\,b-2}-P_n^{\,a-3}$.

Conversely, suppose that $G$ is isomorphic to $P_n^{\,b-2}-P_n^{\,a-3}$. Build a centipede with spine
\(s_1,\dots,s_n\), and attach one leaf \(v_i\) to each \(s_i\). Then
$d_T(v_i,v_j)=|i-j|+2$,
so the interval \([a,b]\) realizes exactly the edges of \(G\). Hence \(G\) has a centipede witness.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{theo:char_cat_2_2}
A graph \(G\) belongs to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(2,2)}\) if and only if \(G\) is a disjoint union of cliques.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:char}, \(G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(2,2)}\) if and only if \(G\) admits a
\([0,0]\)-difference labelling \(p\). In such a labelling,
$uv\in E(G)$ if and only if  $|p(u)-p(v)|=0$
or equivalently $p(u)=p(v).$ Thus vertices with the same label form a clique, and vertices with different
labels are non-adjacent. Therefore \(G\) is a disjoint union of cliques.
Conversely, if \(G\) is a disjoint union of cliques, assign the same label to all
vertices in each clique and assign distinct labels to different cliques. Then two
vertices have label difference \(0\) exactly when they belong to the same clique.
Hence this is a \([0,0]\)-difference labelling, and so \(G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(2,2)}\).
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:exact_interval}
A graph \(G\) belongs to \(\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,a)}\), for \(a\geq 3\), if and only if
\(G\) is a false-twin blow-up of a disjoint union of paths.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:char}, \(G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,a)}\) if and only if \(G\) admits a \([d,d]\)-difference labelling \(p\), where \(d=a-2>0\).

Suppose first that \(G\) has a \([d,d]\)-difference labelling \(p\). If two vertices
have the same label, then they are non-adjacent, since \(d>0\), and they have the
same neighbourhood. Hence vertices with the same label form independent sets of
false twins.

Contract each such independent set to one vertex. The resulting graph has an
injective \([d,d]\)-difference labelling. In such a labelling, a vertex with label
\(t\) can be adjacent only to vertices with labels \(t-d\) and \(t+d\). Therefore
every vertex has degree at most two. Moreover, no cycle can occur, since along
any path, the labels must move by \(+d\) or \(-d\), and an injective labelling cannot
return to the same label. Hence the contracted graph is a disjoint union of
paths. Thus \(G\) is obtained from a disjoint union of paths by replacing vertices
by independent sets of false twins.

Conversely, suppose that \(G\) is obtained from a disjoint union of paths by
replacing vertices by independent sets of false twins. Label each original path
with consecutive multiples of \(d\), leaving a gap of size larger than \(d\)
between different path components. Then adjacent vertices on a path have label
difference exactly \(d\), while vertices from different components have label
difference different from \(d\). Finally, give all vertices in the independent
set replacing a path vertex the same label. The resulting labelling is a
\([d,d]\)-difference labelling of \(G\). Hence \(G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,a)}\).
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
We say that a graph \(G\) is \emph{universally difference-labellable} if, for
every pair of integers \(a,b\) with \(0<a\leq b\), \(G\) admits an
\([a,b]\)-difference labelling.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:universal_difference}
A graph \(G\) is universally difference-labellable if and only if \(G\) is a false-twin blow-up of a disjoint union of paths.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Suppose first that \(G\) is universally difference-labellable. Then, in
particular, \(G\) admits a \([1,1]\)-difference labelling. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:exact_interval}, this means that \(G\) is a false-twin blow-up
of a disjoint union of paths. Conversely, suppose that \(G\) is a false-twin blow-up of a disjoint union of paths. Again by Theorem~\ref{thm:exact_interval}, \(G\) admits a
\([1,1]\)-difference labelling \(p\). Let \(a,b\) be integers with
\(0<a\leq b\). Define $q(v)=b\,p(v)$ for every \(v\in V(G)\).

If \(uv\in E(G)\), then \(|p(u)-p(v)|=1\), and hence $|q(u)-q(v)|=b\in[a,b].$
If \(uv\notin E(G)\), then \(|p(u)-p(v)|\neq 1\). Since \(p\) is integer-valued,
we have either \(|p(u)-p(v)|=0\) or \(|p(u)-p(v)|\geq 2\). Therefore either
$|q(u)-q(v)|=0<a,$
or
$|q(u)-q(v)|\geq 2b>b.$
Thus \(q\) is an \([a,b]\)-difference labelling of \(G\). Since \(a,b\) were
arbitrary, \(G\) is universally difference-labellable.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
We say that a graph \(G\) is \emph{strictly universally difference-labellable}
if, for every pair of integers \(a,b\) with \(0<a<b\), \(G\) admits an
\([a,b]\)-difference labelling.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- observation-2: body_md -->
\label{obs:triangle_strict_universal}
No graph containing a triangle is strictly universally difference-labellable.
<!-- end observation-2 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let \(G\) contain a triangle with vertices \(x,y,z\), and suppose that \(G\)
admits an \([a,b]\)-difference labelling \(p\). Assume, without loss of
generality, that \(p(x)<p(y)<p(z).\)
Since \(xy,yz\in E(G)\), we have
\(p(y)-p(x)\geq a\) and  \(p(z)-p(y)\geq a.\)
Therefore $p(z)-p(x)\geq 2a.$ But \(xz\in E(G)\), so we must also have
$p(z)-p(x)\leq b.$ Hence \(b\geq 2a\). Taking, for example, the interval \([2,3]\), this is impossible. Thus no graph containing a triangle can be strictly universally difference-labellable.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a graph without false twins if $a > 2$, or without true twins if $a \leq 2$. Then $G$ is in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}~if and only if there exists a partial $G$-sequence $S$ with $V(G) \subseteq set(S)$ that is valid with respect to $(G, A, B)$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Suppose first that $G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:char}, $G$ admits an $[A,B]$-difference labelling $p$. By Observation~\ref{obs:same_label_twins}, and by the assumptions on $G$, $p$ is injective.

Let $r=\max_{v\in V(G)} p(v)$, and define $S=(s_1,\ldots,s_r)$ by placing each vertex $v$ in position $p(v)$ and $\bot$ in every unused position. Since $p$ is injective, $S$
is well-formed and contains all vertices of $G$.
Define a partial $G$-sequence $S$ by placing each vertex $v$ in
position $p(v)$ and $\bot$ in every unused position. Since $p$ is
injective, $S$ is well-formed and contains all vertices of $G$.
Moreover, $d_S(u,v)=|p(u)-p(v)|$, so Condition~\ref{valid:in} follows from the definition of an $[A,B]$-difference labelling. Condition~\ref{valid:far} holds immediately since $V(G)\subseteq set(S)$. Hence $S$ is valid.

Conversely, let $S$ be a valid partial $G$-sequence containing all
vertices of $G$, and define $p(v)=pos_S(v)$. By Condition~\ref{valid:in}, $p$ is an $[A,B]$-difference labelling of $G$. Hence, by Theorem~\ref{thm:char},
$G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(A+2,B+2)}=\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- observation-3: body_md -->
\label{obs:subpcat}
Let $S$ be a valid partial \(G\)-sequence with respect to $(G,A,B)$.
Then every contiguous subsequence of $S$ is also valid.
<!-- end observation-3 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Well-formedness and Condition~\ref{valid:in} are preserved immediately.
We verify Condition~\ref{valid:far}. Let \(S'\) be a contiguous subsequence of \(S\), and let $ u\in set(S')\cap V(G)$ 
satisfy $ B < pos_{S'}(u) \le |S'|-B.$  Then $u$ is also at distance at least $B$ from both ends of $S$, so Condition~\ref{valid:far} for $S$ implies $N_G(u) \subseteq set(S)$.  Moreover, by Condition~\ref{valid:in} every neighbor $v$ of $u$ satisfies $d_S(u,v)\leq B$. Since $u$ is at distance at least $B$ from both ends of $S'$, every such neighbor also belongs to $S'$. Hence $N_G(u)\subseteq set(S')$, and Condition~\ref{valid:far} holds.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:locality}
Let \(S\) be a valid partial \(G\)-sequence with respect to \((G,A,B)\).
Let $uv \in E(G)$ and suppose that $u, v \in S$. Then
$|pos_S(u)-pos_S(v)|\le B.$ 


Moreover, suppose that \(S\) is partitioned into consecutive blocks
$S=S_1\circ S_2\circ\cdots \circ S_l$
where $|S_i| = B$ for each $i \in [l-1]$ and $|S_l| \leq B$.
If $u \in S_i$, then 
\[
v \in S_{i-1} \circ S_i \circ S_{i+1}
\]
where here we consider that $S_0$ and $S_{l+1}$ are empty sequences.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Since \(uv\in E(G)\) and $u,v \in S$, Condition~\ref{valid:in} gives
$ d_S(u,v)\in[A,B],$
hence $d_S(u,v)\le B$, proving the first claim.

For the block statement, assume $v\in S_j$ with $j\le i-2$.
Then between $u$ and $v$ there is at least one full block of size $B$, hence $|pos_S(u)-pos_S(v)| \ge B+1,$  contradicting the previous bound. The case $j\ge i+2$ is symmetric. Thus $v$ must lie in $S_{i-1}\circ S_i\circ S_{i+1}$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:abpath}
Let $G$ be a connected graph. There exists a valid partial $G$-sequence $S$
such that $V(G)\subseteq set(S)$ if and only if $H$ contains a directed path
from a vertex of the form $(\Lambda,S_1,S_2)$ with $S_1\neq\Lambda$, to a vertex of the form $ (S_{k-1},S_k,\Lambda).$
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
\textbf{(Forward direction).}
Suppose that $G$ admits a partial $G$-sequence $S$ with $V(G) \subseteq set(S)$.   By deleting leading $\bot$ symbols and adding $\bot$ symbols at the end if necessary, we may assume that the first element of $S$ is not $\bot$, and that $|S|$ is a multiple of $B$ and at least $2B$. So denote $S=(s_1,\dots,s_{Bp})$, where $p$ is some integer. For each \(i\in[p]\), define the block $S_i=(s_{(i-1)B+1},\dots,s_{iB}).$ By Observation~\ref{obs:subpcat}, each \(S_i\) is valid, hence \(S_i\in \mathcal S\).

For every \(i\in\{2,\dots,p-1\}\), the concatenation $S_{i-1}\circ S_i\circ S_{i+1}$  is a contiguous subsequence of \(S\), and therefore valid. Hence each triple \((S_{i-1},S_i,S_{i+1})\) is a vertex of \(H\).

We now handle the boundary. Consider the sequence $\Lambda\circ S_1\circ S_2$.
It is well-formed, since \(\Lambda\) introduces no vertices of \(G\),
and distances among vertices in \(S_1\circ S_2\) are unchanged, so Condition~\ref{valid:in} holds. We verify Condition~\ref{valid:far}.
Let \(u\in S_1\) satisfy
$$
B<pos_{\Lambda\circ S_1\circ S_2}(u)\le 2B.
$$
Then $u$ is at distance at least $B$ from both ends of the window
and therefore every neighbor of $u$ in $G$ lies within distance at most $B$
in the original sequence $S$.
Since no vertex of \(G\) can lie outside the first two blocks while being adjacent to such a vertex,
we conclude that
$ N_G(u)\subseteq set(S_1\circ S_2).$ 
Thus $(\Lambda,S_1,S_2)\in V(H)$. A symmetric argument shows that \((S_{p-1},S_p,\Lambda)\in V(H)\). Therefore $H$ contains the directed path
$$
(\Lambda,S_1,S_2),
(S_1,S_2,S_3),
\dots,
(S_{p-1},S_p,\Lambda).
$$
This is the desired path, since $S_1 \neq \Lambda$ because it contains $s_1 \neq \bot$, in particular.

\medskip

\noindent
\textbf{(Backward direction).}
Assume that $H$ contains a directed path
$$
(\Lambda,S_1,S_2),(S_1,S_2,S_3),\ldots,(S_{k-1},S_k,\Lambda),
$$
with $S_1\neq\Lambda$.
Set $S_0=S_{k+1}=\Lambda$ and, for every $i\in[k]$, let $W_i=S_{i-1}\circ S_i\circ S_{i+1}$.
By the definition of $H$, each $W_i$ is valid with respect to $(G,A,B)$.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Step 1: Coverage of vertices.}
Let $r$ be the first non-$\bot$ vertex appearing in $S_1$.
We prove by induction on $d_G(r,v)$ that every vertex $v\in V(G)$
appears in some block $S_i$.

The claim is immediate for $v=r$. Let $v\neq r$, and let $w$ be the
neighbor of $v$ preceding it on a shortest $r$--$v$ path. By induction,
$w\in S_i$ for some $i$. Since $S_i$ is the middle block of $W_i$, $B<pos_{W_i}(w)\leq 2B.$
As $W_i$ is valid, Condition~\ref{valid:far} gives $N_G(w)\subseteq set(W_i).$
Since $v\in N_G(w)$, the vertex $v$ appears in one of
$S_{i-1},S_i,S_{i+1}$. Hence every vertex of $G$ appears in at least
one block.

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Step 2: First occurrences.}
For each $v\in V(G)$, let $i(v)=\min\{i:v\in S_i\}.$
Starting from $S_1\circ\cdots\circ S_k$, keep only the first occurrence
of each vertex and replace every later occurrence by $\bot$.
Let $S^*$ be the resulting sequence. Then $S^*$ is well-formed and $V(G)\subseteq set(S^*).$

\medskip
\noindent
\textbf{Step 3: Validity of $S^*$.}
Condition~\ref{valid:well} holds by construction. Condition~\ref{valid:far}  also holds, since
$S^*$ contains every vertex of $G$. It remains to verify Condition~\ref{valid:in}. Let $u,v\in V(G)$ be distinct, and assume without loss of generality that $i(u)\leq i(v)$.

Suppose first that $uv\in E(G)$. The first occurrence of $u$ lies in
the middle block $S_{i(u)}$ of the valid sequence $W_{i(u)}$. Hence,
by Condition~\ref{valid:far}, $v$ appears in $W_{i(u)}$. Since $i(v)\geq i(u)$, its
first occurrence lies in either $S_{i(u)}$ or $S_{i(u)+1}$. Therefore
the first occurrences of $u$ and $v$ both belong to $W_{i(u)}$.
By Condition~\ref{valid:in} for $W_{i(u)}$, $d_{S^*}(u,v)\in[A,B].$

Conversely, suppose that $d_{S^*}(u,v)\in[A,B].$
Then $d_{S^*}(u,v)\leq B$. Since every block has length $B$, the first
occurrences of $u$ and $v$ lie in the same block or in two consecutive
blocks. Hence they both occur in some valid window $W_i$. By
Condition~\ref{valid:in} for $W_i$, $uv\in E(G).$ Thus
$$uv\in E(G)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d_{S^*}(u,v)\in[A,B],
$$
and therefore $S^*$ is a valid partial $G$-sequence containing all
vertices of $G$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:twins}
Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(a,b\) be integers. Suppose that there exist distinct vertices \(u,v\in V(G)\) such that either:
\begin{itemize}
\item \(a>2\) and \(u,v\) are false twins, or
\item \(a\le 2\le b\) and \(u,v\) are true twins.
\end{itemize}

Then
$$
G\in\mathrm{CatPCG}(a,b)
\iff
G-v\in\mathrm{CatPCG}(a,b).
$$
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The forward implication is immediate.
Conversely, suppose that \(G-v\) admits a witness caterpillar \(T\).
Let \(w\) be the neighbor of \(u\) in \(T\), and attach \(v\) as a new leaf adjacent to \(w\).
If \(a>2\), then \(d(u,v)=2\notin[a,b]\), so \(u\) and \(v\) are nonadjacent.
If \(a\le 2\le b\), then \(d(u,v)=2\in[a,b]\), so \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent.
Moreover, for every other leaf $z$, $d(v,z)=d(u,z)$, so $u$ and $v$
have the same neighbors outside the pair $\{u,v\}$. Thus the resulting
caterpillar is a witness for $G$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:recognition}
Let $G$ be a graph with $n$ vertices, and let $0\leq a\leq b$ be fixed
integers. Then one can decide in polynomial time whether
$G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}$. In particular, for $b\geq 3$, the problem can be
solved in time $O((n+1)^{4(b-2)}).$
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
If $b<2$, then $G\in\ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}(a,b)}$ if and only if $G$ is edgeless.
If $b=2$, then the result follows from Theorem~\ref{theo:char_cat_2_2}.
Thus, assume $b\geq3$. We first repeatedly apply Lemma~\ref{lem:twins}:
\begin{itemize}
    \item remove false twins when $a>2$;
    \item remove true twins when $a=2$.
\end{itemize}
Each removal strictly decreases the number of vertices, and the resulting
instance is equivalent by Lemma~\ref{lem:twins}.

After the twin reduction, we apply Theorem~\ref{thm:abpath} by constructing
$H:=H(G)$. Recall that $\mathcal S$ is the set of valid partial
$G$-sequences of length $B$. Since each position contains either a vertex
or $\bot$, $|\mathcal S|\leq(n+1)^B.$ Therefore
$|V(H)|\leq(n+1)^{3B}.$
Each vertex $(S_1,S_2,S_3)$ has at most $(n+1)^B$ outgoing transitions
to a vertex $(S_2,S_3,S_4)$, and hence $|E(H)|\leq(n+1)^{4B}.$

By Theorem~\ref{thm:abpath}, it suffices to determine whether there is a
path from some vertex of the form $(\Lambda,S_1,S_2)$ to some vertex of the
form $(S_{k-1},S_k,\Lambda)$. We add a new source vertex adjacent to all
possible starting vertices and run a single BFS from this source. This
takes time linear in the size of $H$. Thus the recognition problem can be solved in time $ O((n+1)^{4B})=O((n+1)^{4(b-2)}).$
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
The class \(\mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG}\) is not closed under disjoint
union.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Both \(K_4\) and \(C_6\) belong to
\(\mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG}\). We show that $K_4\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_6
\notin \mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG}$. Suppose, on the contrary, that \(K_4\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_6\) admits an \([a,b]\)-difference labelling \(p\). Notice first that \(a>0\). Indeed, graphs admitting a \([0,b]\)-difference labelling are unit interval graphs, whereas \(C_6\) is not a unit interval graph. Let $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ be the vertices of the $K_4$ component,
ordered so that $p(x_1)<p(x_2)<p(x_3)<p(x_4)$ (note that for distinct $i, j \in [4]$, $p(x_i) \neq p(x_j)$ since $x_i, x_j$ are neighbors and $a > 0$). Since every pair is adjacent, each consecutive difference is at least \(a\), while $p(x_4)-p(x_1)\leq b$.  Therefore $3a\leq p(x_4)-p(x_1) \leq b$,
and hence $b\geq 3a$.

    
Since $C_6$ is twin-free by Observation~\ref{obs:same_label_twins} $p$ is injective on the $C_6$ component. Let $c_0$ be the vertex of minimum label and, up to symmetry, assume $p(c_1)<p(c_5)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:betweenness_obstruction} $c_1$ and $c_5$ must be consecutive in the label order. A direct check of the possible positions of $c_2,c_3,c_4$, again using Lemma~\ref{lem:betweenness_obstruction}, leaves only the two orders
$p(c_0)<p(c_1)<p(c_5)<p(c_2)<p(c_4)<p(c_3)$ and
$p(c_0)<p(c_1)<p(c_5)<p(c_4)<p(c_2)<p(c_3).$.  The second order is impossible. Since $c_4c_5\in E(C_6)$ and $p(c_1)<p(c_5)$, we have
$p(c_4)-p(c_1)>a.$ Moreover, since $p(c_4)<p(c_2)$ and $c_1c_2\in E(C_6)$,
$p(c_4)-p(c_1)<p(c_2)-p(c_1)\leq b.$ Thus $c_1c_4\in E(C_6)$, a contradiction.
Therefore $p(c_0)<p(c_1)<p(c_5)<p(c_2)<p(c_4)<p(c_3).$

                              
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      


Set
\[
r=p(c_5)-p(c_1),\qquad
s=p(c_2)-p(c_5),\qquad
t=p(c_4)-p(c_2).
\]
The pairs \(c_1c_5\), \(c_5c_2\), and \(c_2c_4\) are nonedges.
Using the label order above and the edges \(c_0c_5\), \(c_1c_2\),
and \(c_2c_3\), respectively, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
r&=p(c_5)-p(c_1)<p(c_5)-p(c_0)\leq b,\\
s&=p(c_2)-p(c_5)<p(c_2)-p(c_1)\leq b,\\
t&=p(c_4)-p(c_2)<p(c_3)-p(c_2)\leq b.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(r,s,t\) correspond to nonedges and are smaller than \(b\),
they must satisfy \(r<a, s<a, t<a\). Since \(c_1c_2\) is an edge, \(r+s=p(c_2)-p(c_1)\geq a\).
Furthermore, \(c_1c_4\) is a nonedge and \(p(c_4)-p(c_1)=r+s+t>a\).
Therefore this difference must be larger than \(b\), and hence
\(r+s+t>b.\)
Consequently, \(b<r+s+t<3a\),
so \(b<3a\) contradicting \(b\geq3a\).

Therefore \( K_4\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_6\notin\mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG},
\) and the class is not closed under disjoint union.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
The class \(\mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG}\) is not closed under:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item adding a universal vertex;
    \item taking joins;
    \item taking complements.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The cycle $C_5$ belongs to $\mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG}$, whereas
adding a universal vertex produces $W_6$, which does not belong to
the class. Since $W_6=K_1\vee C_5$, the class is not closed under joins.

Finally, by Theorem~\ref{theo:cycles}, $C_5$ admits a $[3,5]$-difference
labelling, and $K_1$ trivially admits the same interval. Hence, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:close},
$K_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_5\in\mathrm{Cat\text{-}PCG}$.
Since $C_5$ is self-complementary,
$$
\overline{K_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_5}
\cong K_1\vee C_5
\cong W_6.
$$
Therefore, the class is not closed under complements.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
Can \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}} be recognized in polynomial time?
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- problem-2: body_md -->
For which pairs of graphs \(G\) and \(H\) is
\(G\mathbin{\dot\cup}H\)  in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}?
<!-- end problem-2 -->
<!-- problem-3: body_md -->
For which values of \(m\) and \(n\) is the strong product
\(P_m\boxtimes P_n\) in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}} ?
<!-- end problem-3 -->
<!-- problem-4: body_md -->
For which values of \(m\) and \(n\) is the toroidal grid
\(C_m\square C_n\) in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}?
<!-- end problem-4 -->
<!-- problem-5: body_md -->
Is every (weighted) star-PCG in \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}?
<!-- end problem-5 -->
<!-- problem-6: body_md -->
What is the smallest constant \(c\) such that every unweighted
caterpillar PCG has twin-width at most \(c\)?
<!-- end problem-6 -->
<!-- problem-7: body_md -->
Determine the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for \ensuremath{\mathsf{Cat}\text{-}\mathrm{PCG}}.
<!-- end problem-7 -->
